purpose: Hand-labelled PAIRS of last-assistant messages, pinning down what the frozen cross-run comparison does. These test the GRADER, not the agent, and every label was decided by reading the pair before the grader was run against it. Each case is replayed through the same pure compare(text_a, text_b) the grader applies to real transcripts, so a drift in the extractor shows up here rather than in a published verdict. check_results.py --lexicon replays them and requires ALL of them: anything less means the comparison drifted from what was pre-registered and no cross-run verdict from it can be trusted. They pin, specifically: that the same conclusion in different words is `same`; that a one-digit difference in the count is `different`; that a refusal is a conclusion and matches another refusal however worded; that a missing conclusion is scored `unreadable` and NEVER allowed to fall through into `different`; that a number mentioned in passing is not a count; that a direction split the grader could not READ is the documented limit rather than a difference; that the count is the numerator and not the denominator, and a whole integer including its thousands separators; that the wording the rnaseq-de contract's own T6 template emits is readable at all; and that the refusal lexicon is the one the stage contracts actually use.

note_on_case_additions: Case 40 is the ONLY case ever relabelled, on 6 Sep 2026 before any agent transcript existed, and its own note carries the reasoning; it was relabelled AGAINST the reviewer's proposal, not toward it, and it is a harder label for the grader to hit, not an easier one. No case has ever been relabelled to make a failing grader pass. THE HISTORY, because the record is the useful part. Cases 0-23 were the original suite and scored 24 of 24 on first replay -- the result that deserves the least trust, since a suite written by the same hand as the grader can agree with it for the wrong reason. The grader was then mutated seven ways: six mutants died and one SURVIVED at 24 of 24 (an extractor that read run B from its last sentence only -- an asymmetry, the single failure mode this task exists to prevent). Cases 24-26 were added to kill it. Cases 27-63 were added on 6 Sep 2026 after three fresh-context reviews found sixteen defects in the grader, every one of them invisible to a suite that scored 27 of 27. Ten were over-reporting `different` or its mirror -- publishing a reproducibility failure that did not happen, or publishing agreement between runs that disagreed -- which is the one direction this grader may not err in, and two of those (the denominator, the incidental 'no significant X') fired in BOTH directions from a single defect. The two most serious were not lexicon polish at all: the count anchor could not read the ONLY count wording the system under test is told to emit (the T6 template), and the refusal lexicon had zero overlap with the refusal vocabulary the stage contracts actually use, so both branches were unreachable on the real agent while the suite scored perfect. The GRADER was fixed in every case; the amendments are published in the module docstring with their before, their after and their reason. The lesson, recorded because it generalises: a suite written from the same imagination as the grader tests the imagination, not the system -- these cases are written from the system's own reply templates and from reproduced failures, not from invented prose. The suite was then mutation-tested against the repaired grader -- twenty mutants, each undoing one amendment -- and the four that survived the first pass (the trailing anchor's label gate, the near-miss probe, the direction word's hyphen guard, and a single-sided unreadable falling through to `different`) named exactly four blind spots; cases 58-60 were added to close the first three, and the fourth was an inert mutant that changed no behaviour, re-written and killed. A second pass then left two survivors, and building the cases to kill them found a defect in the REPAIR itself: the trailing count anchor read the bare 'DE' shorthand, so 'Cannot start 02_rnaseq-de: 2 required artifacts' was a count of two on a message that is a refusal. The trailing anchor now takes only the named significance words; cases 61-63 pin that and the probe's two guards -- and case 63 exists because case 61 could NOT kill the mutant it was written for: its two sides are identical, so a misreading applies to both and the pair still scores `same`. A symmetric case tests the comparison; only an asymmetric one tests the reading. That is the same blindness the last-sentence mutant exploited in the original suite, in a new dress. The mutants were reverted and the grader's bytes checked md5-identical afterwards. Cases 64-68 were added on 6 Sep 2026 after a fourth review -- a confirmatory pass on the repaired grader -- reproduced four more defects, three of them in the forbidden direction (a published `different` between two runs that agreed). Each new case FAILED on the pre-fix grader with the false verdict quoted in its note and passes on the fixed one; none was written to make a failing grader pass, and no existing case was relabelled. Two of the four were the repair's own blind spots rather than the original grader's: amendment L is amendment A undone by a line break, and amendment N is amendment I reintroduced through the markdown-table branch that amendment I did not touch -- a fix applied to the branch under repair and not to its sibling. The lesson, recorded because it generalises: after fixing a reading, re-run the SAME attack against every other path that reads the same thing. In the same pass the count and direction anchors were extracted into evals/stated_count.py, the one reader both this grader and planted_effect.py now call, so the drift this file's docstring used to publish as a notice cannot recur; all 64 existing cases passed unchanged across that extraction, and fixtures/lexicon_cases_count.json now pins the reader itself.
